title: Ultrasonic Testing for Oilfield Equipment | UT, US
description: On-site ultrasonic testing for US oilfield and drilling equipment: drill pipe, tubing, vessels, flowlines, forgings. Mobilized to your site. Get a quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Oilfield and Drilling Equipment: Thickness and Forgings
html:
Atlantis NDT performs on-site ultrasonic testing for United States onshore oilfield and drilling equipment: wall thickness on drill pipe and used tubing, production vessels, treaters, flowlines and field tanks, and internal-flaw examination of forgings in hoisting and rig equipment. Technicians are mobilized to the rig yard, the pipe rack, the well site or the production facility. Send the equipment list, material, governing standard and location, and request a UT inspection quote.

What ultrasonic testing answers in upstream operations

Oilfield steel works under abuse that refineries rarely see: cyclic bending, torque, abrasive mud, produced water, carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulfide. Ultrasonic testing answers two practical questions. How much steel is left after corrosion, erosion and wear, and is there an internal flaw in a forged or cast part that surface methods cannot see? For surface cracks at threads, welds and fluid-end bores, magnetic particle testing for oilfield equipment is the companion method, and for non-magnetic hardware liquid penetrant testing for oilfield equipment applies.

This page is about onshore upstream work in the United States. Transmission and gathering pipelines have their own regulatory framework and are covered under ultrasonic testing on pipelines.

The standards that drive upstream inspection

Drilling and well-servicing equipment is covered by a family of API documents. API Specification 5CT governs casing and tubing, API Specification 5DP governs drill pipe, and API Recommended Practice 7G-2 covers the inspection and classification of used drill stem elements. API Recommended Practice 8B covers inspection, maintenance and repair of hoisting equipment, API Recommended Practice 4G addresses drilling and well-servicing structures such as masts and substructures, and API Specification 7K covers drilling and well-servicing equipment. Wellhead and tree components follow API Specification 6A. Production vessels are built to ASME Section VIII, and shop-welded production tanks follow API Specification 12F, with field-welded tanks under API 12D.

Rig contractors and operators sometimes specify a proprietary inspection standard, for example DS-1, and when the customer specifies such a standard we follow the customer’s document and its acceptance rules. State agencies, including the Texas Railroad Commission, the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, CalGEM in California and the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission, regulate well integrity and site conduct, but they do not write NDT procedures; the standards above and the customer’s program do.

What we examine

  • Drill pipe body wall. Thickness readings along the body and in the slip and upset areas where wall thins from wear and corrosion.
  • Used casing and tubing. Wall thickness at spaced points and near the ends, for operators reusing tubing strings or assessing pipe racked for sale.
  • Hoisting and rig forgings. Straight-beam internal examination of hooks, elevators, links, swivel bodies and crown or traveling block components, where the customer’s program calls for it. See ultrasonic testing of castings and forgings.
  • Production vessels and treaters. Thickness surveys on separators, heater treaters, scrubbers and knockouts, with grids at nozzles, the water-oil interface and the bottom.
  • Flowlines and gathering piping. Spot and grid readings at elbows, tees and the 5 to 7 o’clock position of horizontal runs, where produced water settles.
  • Field tanks. Shell thickness on welded and bolted production tanks; larger field tanks may fall under a more formal program, see aboveground storage tank inspection.

Damage mechanisms in the oilfield

Corrosion in produced fluids is driven by carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, chlorides, bacteria and oxygen ingress. Flowline bottoms see channeling corrosion under water; vessel bottoms collect sludge and bacteria. Erosion strikes at chokes, elbows and tees where sand-laden fluid changes direction. Drill pipe wears from rotation against casing and from the slips, and the body wall thins unevenly, so readings at several clock positions matter. Fatigue and cracking are surface issues best caught by other methods, and thickness gauging does not substitute for them.

The right grid follows the mechanism. Uniform corrosion is checked on a coarse grid with extra points at suspected hot spots. Localized and erosive loss needs fine spacing around the pit or elbow. Where sour service raises cracking concerns, thickness readings sit beside a crack check from the other methods, and the hardness and sour-service requirements in NACE MR0175 are part of the customer’s design basis, not something our thickness readings can verify.

Technique in field conditions

We use a calibrated digital thickness gauge with a dual-element probe for corroded steel, calibrated on a step block of matching velocity, and checked at the start and end of every shift and whenever the setup changes. Drill pipe is examined racked and cleaned, with the readings logged against the joint number and the position along the length. Surface conditions in the field matter: mud, paint and scale are wire-brushed or ground to bright metal, and the couplant is chosen for the temperature, because heated production vessels, steam-line tie-ins and cold winter pipe all change the acoustic couplant behavior. Procedures follow ASME Section V, Article 5 for thickness gauging, explained in our Article 5 guide.

Forgings and thick parts are examined with a straight-beam probe, scanned over a marked grid with calibration to a reference block in the customer’s metallurgy, and recorded against a recording level. Acceptance is set by the customer’s standard or the equipment code. Technicians work under the company written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A; Level II technicians perform and interpret, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports.

Drill pipe and tubing in the rack

Used drill pipe is classified by how much wall it has left, how straight it is and whether its connections are sound. Our ultrasonic part of that is the body wall. The joints are laid on racks, cleaned of mud and thread compound, and numbered; readings are taken at set intervals along the tube and at the upset transition, then again at several positions around the circumference, because wear from rotation is rarely uniform. A joint is flagged when the minimum reading falls below the limit in the governing standard or the customer’s specification, and the numbers are handed over without us deciding the class.

Used tubing and casing are checked the same way, with extra attention near the ends where tong marks and thread damage concentrate stress and where internal corrosion often starts at the upset. For tubing strings being recovered after years in a well, scale and wax inside the bore can bias readings from the outside, so we work from the outer surface only and say so in the report. Tubing with pitting patches gets a finer grid across the pit than a smooth tube would, and where the probe face cannot sit flat on a pit edge, the reading is recorded as a limit, not a clean value.

Production vessels, treaters and tanks

Separators, heater treaters, scrubbers and glycol or amine contactors in a field facility are built to ASME Section VIII and may be examined under the operator’s own program or under API 510 where the operator has adopted it. Corrosion concentrates at the bottom of the shell, at the water-oil interface in horizontal separators, around nozzles and at heads, so the thickness grid is laid out with those zones in mind. Fire tubes in heater treaters see their own damage from heat and scale, which an external reading cannot reach; the page does not claim to cover them.

Production tanks built to API 12F or 12D are checked at the lower shell courses, around nozzles and manways, and at the roof-to-shell junction. Floors are a different problem and call for a plan from the tank owner. Bolted tanks present seams and gaskets where ultrasonic readings must avoid joint areas. For larger field tanks that fall under a formal program, NDE support for API 653 tank programs explains how our data feeds the authorized inspector’s decisions.

Reading the numbers: what they do and do not tell you

A thickness reading is a point measurement. The minimum on a grid is a minimum of the points we sampled, not of the entire component, and a missed pit can be thinner than any recorded value. We state the grid spacing and the coverage in the report so the engineer can judge how far to trust it. Readings taken through coating can be several percent off if the instrument is not set for it, so we measure with the coating removed where precision matters and note the condition where it was not.

Temperature adds uncertainty. Sound velocity in steel falls as the metal warms, so a reading on a hot flowline will read thicker than the true value if the instrument was calibrated cold. We calibrate on a block at a temperature close to the work or apply the correction the procedure specifies, and we record surface temperature next to the reading. On steam or heated crude lines, that note is as important as the number.

What the report contains

  • Customer, location, lease or rig, and the equipment tag, serial or joint number.
  • Material, nominal size and wall, and the standard or customer specification governing the inspection.
  • Instrument, probe, couplant, calibration block and calibration checks.
  • The procedure used and its revision, and who approved it.
  • A thickness grid or joint-by-joint table with the minimum reading and the position along the length.
  • Indications from forgings with depth, location and amplitude relative to the reference level.
  • Examiner, qualification level and report reviewer.
  • Acceptance wording only when the customer provides criteria; otherwise the readings stand without disposition.

What to send for a quote

  1. Equipment list by type, size, wall and quantity.
  2. Governing standard or customer specification, including any proprietary inspection standard.
  3. Whether items are racked, installed or in service, and surface temperature.
  4. Coating, cleaning responsibility and any rigging or lifting needed.
  5. Site address, access, H2S or other hazard requirements and orientation steps.
  6. Report format and tagging convention.

Planning realities on US oilfield sites

Lease roads, rain and distance dominate field planning. We ask for the site address and the contact who controls gate access, and we plan equipment and couplant for the temperature extremes of the region. Work near wells can involve hydrogen sulfide, so site orientation and gas detection rules are followed. Drilling rigs run on tight schedules; we coordinate around rig moves and rack changes rather than interrupting operations. Production facilities may be unmanned, so we confirm lockout and communication procedures before starting.

Where we work in the United States

  • Midland: Permian drilling yards, produced-water systems and sour-service facilities.
  • Bakersfield: Kern County heavy-oil facilities with high-temperature surfaces and CalGEM oversight.
  • Oklahoma City: Anadarko Basin rig yards and equipment suppliers.
  • Shreveport: Haynesville high-pressure gas well equipment.
  • Denver: DJ Basin production facilities and tank batteries.
  • San Antonio: Eagle Ford drilling and completion support.
  • Tulsa: drilling contractors, equipment manufacturers and mid-continent producers.
  • Anchorage: Cook Inlet and North Slope facilities with extreme cold.
  • Houston: equipment suppliers and fabrication supporting upstream operations.

What we do not do

We do not perform radiography in the United States and we are not a drill-stem inspection yard with fixed full-length inspection lines. Specialist techniques for crack sizing and long-length screening are outside this page, and we do not calculate remaining life or fitness for service. See pressure vessel inspection services for vessel programs and NDE support for API 510 programs.

Training your own technicians

Drilling contractors and producers can build in-house skill through UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with the ultrasonic simulator and oil and gas NDT training. Employers certify their own people under SNT-TC-1A.

faq.q: What can ultrasonic testing measure on drill pipe?
faq.a: It measures remaining wall thickness in the body and slip area, which thins from wear and corrosion. Cracks at connections are a surface question that magnetic particle inspection answers, so the two methods are often scheduled together.

We can follow API RP 7G-2 or the customer-specified inspection standard for the ultrasonic and magnetic work we perform. We are not a drill-stem inspection yard with fixed inspection lines, so confirm scope against the document.

faq.q: Can you check hoisting equipment forgings?
faq.a: Yes. Straight-beam ultrasonic examination of hooks, elevators and swivel bodies can reveal internal flaws, with acceptance set by the customer program and API RP 8B practice. Surface cracks on the same parts need magnetic particle inspection.

faq.q: How do you inspect flowlines in produced water service?
faq.a: We take grid readings at elbows, tees and the 5 to 7 o’clock position of horizontal runs where produced water settles. Findings go to your engineer, who decides on repair or replacement.
We follow site H2S rules and gas detection requirements. Thickness readings do not verify material hardness or sour-service compliance, which the customer’s design basis and NACE MR0175 address.

State agencies such as the Texas Railroad Commission, Oklahoma Corporation Commission, CalGEM and the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission oversee wells and sites, while API standards and the customer’s program set the NDT requirements.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects readings or indications?
faq.a: The customer or its engineer does, using the standard or specification it names. We report thickness, location and any indications with the reference level so that decision can be made.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote?
faq.a: The equipment list with size, wall and quantity, the governing standard, location and site address, condition and temperature, cleaning responsibility, hazards and orientation requirements, and the report format.

faq.q: Do you offer radiography or advanced inspection?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and specialist techniques are not offered on this page. We perform ultrasonic, magnetic particle and liquid penetrant work, with Level III review of procedures.
